outputs.L1: A clip-on microphone assembly is provided, comprising: a clip-on mechanism (16) for attaching the microphone assembly (10) to a user’s clothing (11); at least three microphones (20, 21, 22) for capturing audio signals from the user’s voice, the microphones defining a microphone plane; an acceleration sensor (32) for generating an orientation signal by sensing gravitational acceleration in at least two orthogonal dimensions; and an audio signal-processing unit (34) for producing an output audio signal (36) from the captured audio signals. The audio signal-processing unit comprises: a beamformer unit (24) configured to process the captured audio signals to generate the output audio signal in a manner that creates a directional acoustic beam; a direction-of-arrival (DOA) unit (30) configured to determine the direction of arrival of sound by analyzing the captured audio signals; and a control unit (26) configured to control the beamformer unit. The control unit is adapted to determine, based on the orientation signal, an allowed angular sector (40) for the direction of the acoustic beam and to steer the acoustic beam within the allowed angular sector according to the determined direction of arrival.
outputs.L2:
A wearable microphone assembly (10) includes a fastening clip (16) that secures the assembly to a user’s (11) clothing. The assembly has three or more microphones (20, 21, 22), arranged to define a microphone plane, for detecting audio from the user’s voice. It also incorporates an acceleration sensor (32) that measures gravitational acceleration along at least two perpendicular axes and generates an orientation signal.

An audio-processing unit (34) derives an output audio signal (36) from the detected signals. This unit includes a beamformer (24), which processes the microphone signals to form a directional acoustic beam, and a direction-of-arrival unit (30), which analyzes those signals to identify the direction from which sound is received. A controller (26) operates the beamformer by using the orientation signal to establish a permitted angular range (40) for the beam and steering the beam within that range based on the identified sound-arrival direction.
outputs.L3:
The clip-on microphone assembly is designed to attach securely to a user’s clothing by means of a clip-on mechanism. The assembly includes at least three microphones configured to capture the user’s voice. The microphones are spatially arranged to define a microphone plane, enabling directional audio processing.

An acceleration sensor integrated into the assembly determines its orientation by detecting gravitational acceleration along at least two orthogonal dimensions. Based on the measured acceleration, the system can establish the orientation of the microphone plane relative to gravity and, consequently, relative to the user.

An audio processing unit processes the signals received from the microphones using beamforming and direction-of-arrival analysis. The direction-of-arrival analysis identifies the direction from which a sound, such as the user’s voice, is received, while the beamforming process combines the microphone signals to enhance audio originating from a selected direction and suppress unwanted sounds from other directions.

A control unit uses the determined orientation to define an allowed angular sector in which the user’s voice is expected to originate. The control unit then directs the audio processing unit to steer the acoustic beam within that sector toward the detected sound direction. In this manner, the assembly produces an output audio signal with improved voice clarity and reduced interference from ambient noise.
outputs.L4:
A clip-on microphone assembly is designed to capture a wearer’s voice clearly even when the assembly is attached to clothing in different positions or orientations. The assembly includes an array of at least three spatially separated microphones, an acceleration sensor, and signal-processing circuitry. The microphones receive acoustic signals from multiple directions, while the acceleration sensor supplies information that can be used to estimate the assembly’s orientation relative to gravity and, consequently, its likely position on the wearer.

During operation, signals from the microphones are analyzed to determine the direction of arrival of a sound source, such as the wearer’s speech. The orientation information from the acceleration sensor defines an angular sector in which the wearer’s mouth is expected to be located. Direction-of-arrival processing may then be restricted to that sector, reducing the likelihood that noises or competing speakers outside the expected region will be mistaken for the desired source.

After a likely voice direction has been identified, a beamformer combines the microphone signals with suitable delays, phases, or weighting factors. This creates a directional acoustic pickup pattern that is steered toward the detected sound source. The beam may also be constrained so that its steering direction remains within the orientation-based angular sector. As the wearer moves, or as the clip-on assembly changes position on the clothing, the sensor and microphone data can be evaluated repeatedly to update the sector, source direction, and beamforming parameters.

By integrating physical-orientation sensing with acoustic direction finding, the assembly can adapt to variations in how it is worn rather than relying on a fixed microphone direction. Steering the beam toward the wearer’s voice increases the level and intelligibility of the desired speech, while restricting the beam and attenuating signals from other directions suppresses ambient noise, reverberation, and unwanted speakers. The resulting output is therefore better suited for voice communication, recording, transcription, voice-command recognition, and similar speech-processing applications.

The package was there, resting beneath the flickering light at the end of the corridor. No label, no return address—only three letters stamped across the top in red ink: **DOA**.

Mara hesitated before opening it. Inside, she found an old watch, its hands frozen at midnight, and a note that read: *You were supposed to be there.*

Then the watch began to tick.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style independent claim for a clip-on microphone assembly that uses at least three microphones, an accelerometer, direction-of-arrival analysis, and orientation-aware beam steering.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for a wearable microphone clipped to a user’s clothing, where gravitational acceleration determines an allowed angular sector and a beamformer tracks the detected voice direction within that sector.
counterfactuals.output:
A wearable audio device comprises a microphone array, an inertial sensor, and a processor in a housing configured to clip to a user’s clothing. The inertial sensor measures gravitational acceleration to determine the device’s orientation relative to vertical. Based on that orientation, the processor defines an allowed angular sector corresponding to a region in which the wearer’s mouth is expected to be located.

The microphone array detects acoustic energy from multiple directions. A direction-of-arrival estimator identifies a candidate voice direction, and a beamformer steers its acoustic beam toward that direction only when it lies within the allowed angular sector. As the user moves, the processor continuously updates both the sector from the measured gravity vector and the beam direction from detected speech, thereby tracking the wearer’s voice while attenuating sounds arriving from outside the sector.

The sector may be defined by azimuth and elevation limits, adjusted for the clip position or calibrated to the wearer. Confidence measures, voice-activity detection, and temporal smoothing may prevent abrupt beam changes or tracking of competing speakers.

counterfactuals.prompt: How could a lavalier microphone system automatically steer an acoustic beam toward the wearer’s voice while preventing the beam from pointing in implausible directions when the clip rotates? Answer in patent language and include reference numerals.
counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a lavalier microphone system **(100)** comprises a housing **(102)** configured to be attached to a garment by a rotatable clip **(104)**. A microphone array **(110)** disposed in the housing **(102)** includes a plurality of spatially separated acoustic transducers **(112A–112D)**. A beamformer **(120)** applies respective delays and/or complex weights to microphone signals to define a steerable acoustic reception beam **(122)**.

An orientation sensor **(130)**, which may comprise an accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, clip-angle encoder, or combination thereof, generates orientation data representative of rotation of the housing **(102)** and/or clip **(104)**. A voice-direction estimator **(140)** determines one or more candidate directions of arrival **(142)** from the microphone signals. The candidate directions may be determined using time-difference-of-arrival processing, phase correlation, acoustic-energy comparison, or a learned voice-localization model.

A constraint processor **(150)** maintains a wearer-relative admissible steering region **(152)** corresponding to physically plausible locations of the wearer’s mouth relative to an attachment location **(154)**. The admissible steering region **(152)** may comprise a cone, angular sector, or probabilistic spatial distribution extending generally upwardly and inwardly from the attachment location **(154)**. The constraint processor **(150)** transforms the admissible steering region **(152)** from a wearer coordinate frame **(156)** into an array coordinate frame **(158)** using the orientation data. Accordingly, rotation of the clip **(104)** rotates the permissible region in array coordinates without causing the permissible region to rotate away from the wearer in wearer coordinates.

A steering controller **(160)** selects a steering direction **(162)** by combining the candidate directions **(142)** with the transformed admissible steering region **(152)**. A candidate direction outside the admissible steering region may be rejected, projected onto a boundary of the admissible steering region, or assigned a reduced probability. In an embodiment, the steering direction is determined according to:

\[
\hat{\mathbf d}=\arg\max_{\mathbf d \in \mathcal{R}}
\left[C_{\mathrm{voice}}(\mathbf d)\,P_{\mathrm{mouth}}(\mathbf d)\right],
\]

where \(\mathcal{R}\) is the orientation-corrected admissible steering region, \(C_{\mathrm{voice}}\) is an acoustic confidence value, and \(P_{\mathrm{mouth}}\) is a prior probability that the wearer’s mouth lies in direction \(\mathbf d\).

The steering controller **(160)** may further employ temporal filtering, angular-rate limits, hysteresis, and a hold state. Thus, when acoustic confidence falls below a threshold, the beamformer **(120)** maintains a preceding valid direction or steers toward a nominal wearer-relative direction **(164)** rather than following an interferer. Directions corresponding to a downward direction, an outward direction away from the wearer, a rearward direction through the wearer’s torso, or another anatomically implausible direction may thereby be excluded.

In certain embodiments, a calibration processor **(170)** estimates a mounting pose of the clip **(104)** from gravity, detected speech, and/or an initialization utterance. The calibration processor **(170)** may adapt the admissible steering region **(152)** over time while retaining predetermined anatomical limits **(172)**. The resulting system automatically directs the acoustic reception beam **(122)** toward the wearer’s voice while remaining substantially invariant to rotation or reorientation of the lavalier housing **(102)**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a patent-abstract-style paragraph for an orientation-aware clip-on microphone assembly that determines sound direction from captured signals and controls beamforming according to both DOA and accelerometer data.
counterfactuals.output: An orientation-aware clip-on microphone assembly includes a housing configured for attachment to a user or article, a plurality of spatially separated acoustic transducers, an accelerometer configured to generate orientation or motion data, and a processor operatively coupled thereto. The processor receives captured audio signals from the acoustic transducers, determines a direction of arrival (DOA) of sound based on relative characteristics of the captured signals, and determines an orientation or movement state of the assembly from the accelerometer data. A beamforming controller selects or adjusts one or more beamforming parameters, including beam direction, beam width, transducer weighting, delay, gain, or noise-suppression characteristics, according to both the determined DOA and the orientation or movement state. The processor may transform the DOA between assembly-relative and environment-relative coordinate frames, compensate for changes caused by rotation or displacement of the clip-on assembly, and maintain or redirect an acoustic pickup beam toward a target sound source. The assembly thereby provides adaptive directional audio capture despite variations in mounting position, wearer posture, or movement.
